source_read: PMC HTML, PMC13623016 (author manuscript of the version published before final editing, Inj Prev 13 Aug 2026, ip-2025-046028), read in full in the reader's own browser tab (title confirmed): abstract, background, methods, results with Tables 1–2, discussion, conclusions, key messages, references. Figures 1–2 (flowchart, map) not viewed: no claim value is printed only in a figure. Table 1 percentages recomputed by the reader.

claims.overstatement: None, except that 'an autopsy' here includes partial autopsies, which matters beside a claim about full autopsies.
claims.note: 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine states, 2019–2021: autopsy 67.4% (Table 1 'Any' column 37,346; the medical-examiner and coroner columns sum to 37,436 = 67.5%, and the printed SD fits 37,436, so the 'Any' count looks transposed; 'about 67%' holds either way), opioid test recorded 44,011 (79.4%), alcohol test 42,128 (76.0%). Points for the editor: (1) autopsy means full or partial (Methods 5th paragraph; Results 6th paragraph); suggest 'a full or partial autopsy'; (2) the paper says 'no' and 'unknown' were counted together for the opioid and alcohol tests only; it does not say how a missing autopsy entry was coded; (3) the authors note tests may have been done without the information reaching abstractors, so these are shares recorded, as the claim says; (4) recorded testing differed by system for alcohol (84.5% in medical-examiner against 58.6% in coroner counties) but not for opioids (79.3% against 79.6%) or autopsy (67.1% against 68.4%), a small piece of evidence that testing practice varies between offices; (5) the deaths combine NVDRS (suicide, undetermined) and SUDORS (unintentional) records from a convenience sample of states.

anchors.extracted: Nine states (Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Maryland, Minnesota, North Carolina, Washington, Wisconsin), deaths 2019–2021: 3,080 suicides and 3,887 undetermined (NVDRS) plus 48,463 unintentional overdoses (SUDORS) = 55,430. Autopsy recorded 37,346 (67.4%; column parts sum to 37,436), opioid toxicology test 44,011 (79.4%; text 79%), alcohol test 42,128 (76.0%; text 76%).

For the opioid and alcohol test indicators, 'no' and 'unknown' were both coded as not tested, since either means the abstractor lacked the information; the autopsy indicator covers a full or partial autopsy.

Medical-examiner counties (37,198) against coroner counties (18,232): alcohol test recorded 31,444 (84.5%) against 10,684 (58.6%); opioid test 29,499 (79.3%) against 14,512 (79.6%); autopsy 24,969 (67.1%) against 12,467 (68.4%). Reader's percentages.

Limitations: convenience sample of states, may not generalize; tests coded as not done may have been done without the information being available to abstractors; unmeasured confounders such as office funding.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement: the claim reports odds ratios as odds, keeps the reversed pooled result, and says no study checked which records were right; the authors' own wording (a strong association) is stronger than the claim's.
claims.note: All Lundberg numbers check: OR 1.79 (1.43–2.27) with state and year fixed effects; 1.52 (1.20–1.95), 1.61 (1.26–2.06) and 1.60 (1.25–2.05) as county, investigation and decedent controls are added; 0.32 (0.29–0.35) without state effects (crude OR from Table 1 counts 0.321); 558 of 18,232 (3.1%) against 3,329 of 37,198 (8.9%) undetermined; alcohol test 58.6% against 84.5%; autopsy 68.4% against 67.1%; opioid test 79.6% against 79.3%; system type from a CDC listing dated 30 August 2024 (accessed January 2025). Points for the editor: (1) a 'coroner county' is any county the listing classes as a non-medical-examiner system; (2) with state fixed effects the 1.79 can only come from states with both kinds of county; by the paper's own description Indiana is all coroner and North Carolina and Maryland have central medical examiners, so at most six of the nine states contribute (reader's inference; Figure 1 not viewed); (3) undetermined and suicide deaths come from NVDRS and accidental deaths from SUDORS; the paper does not report whether both systems covered the same counties, which would matter for the comparison; (4) the pooled reversal is attributed to Maryland without a model that drops Maryland; (5) whether a test was recorded made little difference (opioid OR 1.14, 1.00–1.29; alcohol 1.00, 0.86–1.17), so the alcohol-testing gap does not account for the association; (6) reporting slips that do not change the claim: Table 2's significance legend is reversed (three stars labelled the 0.05 level), and the Discussion places the autopsy and test controls in model (3) although the Methods and Table 2 put them in model (4).

anchors.extracted: Logistic regression of undetermined intent against suicide or unintentional overdose among drug poisoning deaths; suicide and undetermined deaths from the NVDRS restricted file, unintentional deaths from SUDORS (each manner available in only one system); nine states chosen as a convenience sample and for variation in systems; deaths 2019–2021, any age. County system from a CDC listing (ref 22, dated 30 August 2024); coroner indicator = any non-medical-examiner system.

Model 1 (year fixed effects only): coroner OR 0.32 (0.29–0.35), i.e. fewer undetermined classifications in coroner counties, which the authors attribute to Maryland (central medical examiner, unusually many undetermined deaths). Model 2 (state and year fixed effects, within-state comparison): OR 1.79 (1.43–2.27).

anchors.extracted: Adding county population, poverty, unemployment and rurality: OR 1.52 (1.20–1.95); adding autopsy, opioid and alcohol tests, suicide note and investigator narrative: 1.61 (1.26–2.06); adding age, sex and race: 1.60 (1.25–2.05), n = 55,423. In model 5, opioid test recorded OR 1.14 (1.00–1.29), alcohol test 1.00 (0.86–1.17), autopsy 1.27 (1.12–1.44).

Medical-examiner counties 37,198 deaths, coroner counties 18,232 (32.9%). Undetermined 3,329 (8.9%) against 558 (3.1%); alcohol test recorded 31,444 (84.5%) against 10,684 (58.6%); autopsy 24,969 (67.1%) against 12,467 (68.4%); opioid test 29,499 (79.3%) against 14,512 (79.6%). Reader's percentages.

anchors.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Methods, 6th paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Preferred models use state indicators so that results reflect variation between county systems within states; Indiana relies only on county coroners and North Carolina has a central medical examiner (Maryland likewise central), so these states give no within-state contrast. Across models 2–5 the lower 95% bound never fell below 1.20; authors read this as at least 52% higher odds in coroner counties.

Test-recorded indicators largely non-significant, so testing resources do not explain the association; authors suggest suicides may be under-reported in coroner counties if some undetermined deaths are suicides, but no classification was checked against another source; limitations: convenience sample, no funding measure, other confounders possible, 2019–2021 overlaps the COVID-19 strain on offices.

Death investigation is not standardized: 22 states use central or county/district medical examiners, the rest coroners or a county mix (CDC page, 2019); medical examiners are typically appointed physicians and coroners elected laypeople, but some states require coroners to be physicians and others require forensic pathologists for autopsies.
